Qualcomm executives this summer introduced an architecture called high-bandwidth computing (HBC), the solution to an ongoing problem in AI inferencing – and now in agentic AI – that they and others call the memory wall. Essentially, the performance of these models increasingly depends less on the compute capability of a processor – how fast the chip can calculate – and more on how quickly the chip can feed data to the calculation.It’s an issue that affects both the performance of the AI model as well as the cost for running the AI workloads. Qualcomm outlined two strategies that are widely used – one that houses the AI model in fast on-chip memory, and another that uses stacked high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to support a processor. Qualcomm advocates a third strategy – near-memory computing, or HBC – that moves the computer closers to the all-important memory.

Executives argue that to close a widening gap – to remove the memory wall – between the need for more compute and the ability to feed that demand with data, the compute needs to move closer to the memory and the data it holds. It gives the AI model faster access to the data it needs, and reduces the time, energy, and cost that come when the data needs to travel a longer distance to get to the compute.It’s an argument Qualcomm made in July when first pitching the HBC architecture, and one they continue to make now.“In traditional computer architecture, you usually have DDR, you have memory of package, you have usually plenty of capacity on that, but you have a narrow link, which moves the data very slowly,” Gerardo Giaretta, vice president and general manager of datacenter CPU and AI at Qualcomm, recently told journalists and analysts. “So far, AI has been really focusing on the HBM architecture. It basically increases the number of lanes and how fast you can move the data between the compute and the HBM. The challenge with that is the premium you're going to pay for HBM, a premium in terms of the cost of the solution that goes in particular on the amount of power that HBM consumes and a complex interposer and 2.5D packaging, co-host packaging and so forth.”That moving of the data to the compute side of things and back is the problem HBC – moving the compute next to where the data is stored – is solving, Giaretta argued.

“You have in-package, you have a stack of memory – in our case, LPDDR-based – and you have a compute die under the stack of memory,” he said. “Basically, you don't have to move the data anymore [in] packets. You automatically have a very, very high bandwidth between the memory and the compute and you have strong energy savings simply because now you're not moving data across millimeters, but you're moving data or across micrometers. Simply, the amount of space that the data traverses is much less, and that results in much better energy consumption as well as energy efficiency.”Diving a bit deeper, Giaretta said in the first generation of HBC, Qualcomm uses the LPDDR stack and a full AI accelerator under the stack, where most of the operations for the AI workloads are done. Some operations may move to the central system-on-a-chip (SOC) – which is the vendor’s Dragonfly AI250 – depending on the architecture and its implementation. That said, most of the processing stays within the HBC package.The AI250 – Qualcomm has started production of the AI inference platform, which is due for release next year – has significantly more TFLOPs, and the interface between the AI250 and LPDDR is slower than HBC. The key is to instruct the HBC to do what it needs to do, he said,“You should think about HPC in that particular implementation as a co-processor, as a coexistent,” Giaretta said. “Once you instruct that, and the majority of the decode operations are done within HBC, then your end-to-end performance is not affected by this slower link, because you just send back results. You don't have to send the data, you just have to send the results."

Since July, Qualcomm experts have been outlining the inferencing challenges that HBC will address. This week, the company announced that it now has first-generation HBC silicon in the lab, with its complete memory read-write path and near-memory computations at production levels validated in tests. Qualcomm engineers used industry-standard automated test equipment (ATE) for the validation efforts. What the testing found is that HBC can deliver as much as 18 times the memory bandwidth vs. LPDDR, and an energy-efficiency measurement of five times the terabit-per-second-per-watt compared to HBM4, the sixth-generation of high-bandwidth memory.“You can really do inference, and it drives a clear performance advantage on the solution,” Giaretta said of the results. “As we said at the beginning, AI inference is not only – but for the majority part – memory bandwidth-bound limited. This solution gives you the bandwidth that you need at the lowest energy. ... From an OPEX perspective, the energy efficiency – really the amount of energy that you spend moving the data – is at least one order of magnitude less.”With the results in hand, Qualcomm is moving forward with its plans. Qualcomm for more than a year has been playing out plans to become a larger player in the AI datacenter space and an alternative to Nvidia. Now HBC will be integrated into Dragonfly AI250 to create what executives say will be a full AI inference accelerator platform, which will be foundational to the Qualcomm Dragonfly Rack, the vendor’s full stack infrastructure for inference workloads. The AI250 is expected to start sampling in the first half of 2027.

The validation of the HBC silicon also is the first step of a multi-year roadmap, with the sampling of the AI250 and the upcoming Dragonfly C1000 CPUs both set for next year and samples of the Dragonfly AI300 coming in 2028.The validation “is particularly important for us because HBC is a clear differentiator of our solution versus others,” Giaretta said. “Our solution is not just memory. That's why we call it HBC, high-bandwidth compute. We have compute, with the real TFLOPs under the memory stack. Our solution is not just improving the memory bandwidth. Our solution is putting the compute just under the memory so that you have better memory bandwidth.”He also noted that Qualcomm is working with various partners to determine the different ways HBC can be used. The Dragonfly AI250 isn’t the only products where it will be used.The validation of the HBC silicon also should erase doubts about whether Qualcomm can keep its promise of high-yield manufacturing of the AI250 next year, he said. “I's important to understand that this is not a normal chip,” Giaretta said. “This is the first time that somebody has done something like this. We usually don't do a blog or a pre-briefing and so forth for a bring-up of a chip. We do gazillions of chips in Qualcomm and we don't do that. The reason why we decided to do that is exactly because it's completely new technology and it's a good validation of what we will see next year in terms of high-yield manufacturing.” ®
